newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yen pulled in opposing directions - Sakakibara.
newsitem.headline: Yen pulled in opposing directions - Sakakibara.

text.p: The yen is being pulled in opposite directions by two factors that need to be watched in determining the currency's outlook, Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said in a television interview broadcast on Monday.

"The market for the yen is being pulled lower by financial globalisation which will result from Japan's 'Big Bang' reforms and pushed higher by pressures which come from the expansion of Japan's current account surplus," Sakakibara told an economic seminar hosted by Shizuoka Dai-ichi Television in southwest Japan.
"We must watch both factors closely before determining what the outlook for the yen is," said Sakakibara, Vice Finance Minister of International Affairs.
Commenting on whether Japan's "Big Bang" financial and economic reforms would cause Japanese capital to move overseas, Sakakibara said some assets were certain to flow out of Japan.
But, he added, since foreign investments tended to be of the high-risk, high-return nature, it was unlikely that a massive amount of Japanese money would pour into overseas investments.

Sakakibara said that, since so many Japanese used part of their income on overseas trips in recent years, "I think it would be appropriate for Japanese people to have overseas holdings of the equivalent amount of money they spend on holidays in foreign countries."

On the development of Japanese financial markets after the implementation of the "Big Bang" reforms, Sakakibara said it depended on how domestic and foreign investment trusts expanded their businesses here.

Investment trusts are equivalent to mutual funds in the United States and Britain's unit trusts. The "Big Bang" is intended to allocate Japan's 1,200 trillion yen ($10.43 trillion) in individual financial assets more effectively.
Foreign securities houses with experience in developing attractive investment products are keen to expand into investment trusts and asset management in Japan.
Sakakibara said that as a result of the "Big Bang," more large mergers were likely between Japanese and foreign companies.
"The companies most affected by the 'Big Bang' will be the large brokers, large banks and large insurers," he added.
